definition: Simulation in Philip K. Dick's exegesis is the camouflage by which Valis "invades" and overlays the world (CLM_S_4b73c120df). The frame is theological rather than technological: PKD tests it against Brahman / Maya and reincarnation (CLM_S_60e8d345f3), and reads Christ as "self injected into a simulation, a program being run" (CLM_S_55d9aed585).
pkd_relevance: Simulation is one of PKD's defining concepts, present from *Time Out of Joint* (1959) through *Ubik* (1969) to the late exegesis. What sets PKD's framing apart from contemporary "we-might-be-in-a-simulation" speculation is its theological grounding: the simulated layer is not arbitrary software but Valis's "camouflage" of an underlying reality that is itself first-century Christian (CLM_S_4b73c120df). PKD treats Brahmanism — Brahman, Maya, reincarnation — as the closest analogue (CLM_S_60e8d345f3) and inverts the moral valence: the simulated USA "serves a benign purpose: the posing of the moral problem" (CLM_S_7a504dee41). Christ, on this reading, is "authentic — i.e. living — self injected into a simulation, a program being run" (CLM_S_55d9aed585).
in_the_fiction: PKD's fiction is saturated with simulation scenarios. In Time Out of Joint (1959), Ragle Gumm discovers his small-town life is an elaborate construct. In The Man in the High Castle (1962), the I Ching suggests that the Axis-victory world may itself be a fiction. Ubik (1969) presents nested levels of simulated reality in half-life. These works establish simulation not as a single plot device but as PKD's fundamental narrative architecture.
in_the_exegesis: Simulation in the exegesis is theological, not technological. PKD's own gloss: "the reason PKD writes about simulated reality (or reality as simulation) is that Valis has invaded our reality and is simulating it — what PKD called camouflage" (CLM_S_4b73c120df). When he tests the idea, he licenses it through Brahmanic precedent — "this idea that we're in a simulated reality (which Valis generates and controls) seems less unlikely when one considers Brahmanism: Brahman, Maya, reincarnation" (CLM_S_60e8d345f3). The frame inverts the usual one: Christ is "authentic — i.e. living — self injected into a simulation, a program being run" (CLM_S_55d9aed585). Even the apparent USA of 1974, "simulated though it is, serves a benign purpose: the posing of the moral problem" (CLM_S_7a504dee41). The Parousia, on this reading, has been "obscured by spurious changes — a simulated world-process" (CLM_S_5f5cd81168).
intellectual_background: PKD's simulation concept draws on Plato's cave allegory, Gnostic cosmology (the demiurge as reality-fabricator), Buddhist and Hindu concepts of Maya, and Baudrillard's simulacra theory. The concept anticipates later 'simulation hypothesis' arguments by Bostrom and others, though PKD's version is theologically rather than computationally grounded.
scholarly_debate: Scholars debate whether PKD's simulation theme is primarily epistemological (how do we know what is real?) or ontological (what is the nature of reality itself?). Baudrillard cited PKD as a key precursor. Critics like Fitting emphasize the political dimension — simulation as ideology — while Davis and Kripal read the theme through religious studies as a modern Gnostic revelation narrative.
chronology_summary: Simulation themes appear in PKD's earliest work but intensify after 2-3-74, when the fictional device became a personal conviction. The Exegesis passages on simulation are concentrated in the 1976-1981 period.
contradictions_summary: PKD oscillates between treating simulation as a prison to be escaped and as a necessary structure maintained by the divine for pedagogical purposes. The Exegesis also wavers between Platonic (reality as shadow of the Forms) and Gnostic (reality as trap set by the demiurge) frameworks, which carry different ethical implications.
editorial_notes: The simulation theme overlaps heavily with False Reality and Reality Testing topics. Researchers should cross-reference these entries and note that PKD's simulation concept is theological rather than computational.
open_questions: Does PKD's simulation concept ultimately resolve into a Platonic, Gnostic, or uniquely Dickian framework?
How does the simulation theme in the fiction differ structurally from the simulation claims in the Exegesis?
What is the relationship between PKD's simulation ideas and his amphetamine use in the 1960s-70s?

definition_legacy: Simulation in PKD's work refers to the possibility that experienced reality is a constructed, projected, or counterfeit version of a deeper or truer reality — a theme that bridges his science fiction, his Gnostic theology, and his personal experiences of ontological uncertainty.
pkd_relevance_legacy: Simulation is one of PKD's most persistent and philosophically significant themes. From the fake worlds of Time Out of Joint and The Man in the High Castle to the half-life of Ubik and the Black Iron Prison of the Exegesis, PKD repeatedly constructs narratives in which characters discover that their perceived reality is fabricated. After 2-3-74, this fictional theme became a lived conviction: PKD came to believe that the Roman Empire had never ended and that contemporary reality was a simulation overlaying the true apostolic world.
in_the_exegesis_legacy: The Exegesis treats simulation as an ontological proposition rather than a fictional device. PKD theorizes that the phenomenal world is a 'dokos' (Greek for semblance), a hologrammatic projection generated by the Black Iron Prison to conceal the true Palm Tree Garden reality beneath. He draws on Platonic, Gnostic, and Vedantic frameworks to describe layers of simulation, and connects his 2-3-74 experience to the moment when the simulated veil was momentarily pierced.
